video_title: Why Claude can’t be your PM (yet) | Anthropic CPO Panel
gist: Anthropic product leaders (Amy and Mike) at a Lenny's Podcast live panel argue the PM role persists as a convenor/judgment function even as building gets cheap, describe agent-native and malleable software, and explain how Anthropic runs overlapping bets, evals for parked projects, and consolidation.

insights.claim: Anthropic's product leadership argues the PM role is not disappearing: the technology changes every two months while human problems change slowly, so the PM job of bridging real human problems and current technology persists.
insights.speaker: Amy (Anthropic product leader)
insights.so_what: AI-driven PM obsolescence narrative is overstated; the bridge function persists.
insights.quote: the technology side is changing but the human side like the human side doesn't change that fast

insights.claim: At Anthropic, a builder who moved to an IC role and assumed Claude could cover product management found a dedicated PM was still needed to supply glue and connective tissue, such as enabling customer success, safeguards and keeping people on track, before a launch serving prosumers through large enterprises.
insights.speaker: Mike (Anthropic builder)
insights.so_what: Even at the most AI-native firm, launch coordination across customer segments is still a human job.
insights.quote: all of the things and all the glue and all of the connective tissue

insights.claim: Because AI lets teams move faster, the coordinating PM role requires greater operational excellence than before, and Anthropic sees this hat as increasingly important when recruiting for teams.
insights.speaker: Mike (Anthropic builder)
insights.so_what: Operational execution, not ideation, is the scarce PM skill.

insights.claim: Anthropic's leaders say Claude is not yet a convenor: no one has seen Claude schedule a meeting among humans unprompted, though the limit is a settings choice rather than capability, and the 'convenor' is one archetype for the human role in a post-powerful-AI world.
insights.speaker: Mike (Anthropic builder)
insights.so_what: Agentic coordination across people is a near-term capability that is gated by product choices, not models.

insights.claim: In a world where building is cheap and fast, the scarce skills are judgment about what to build on limited information and relentlessness in execution amid many forking paths.
insights.speaker: Amy (Anthropic product leader)
insights.so_what: Hiring and evaluation should shift toward judgment and follow-through.
insights.quote: judgment in the face of ambiguity

themes.theme: Skills made obsolete by cheap building

insights.claim: A veteran product leader says the skill of agonizing over interaction details, such as button placement and thumb reach, is now obsolete because building three versions and testing them is faster than debating.
insights.speaker: Amy (Anthropic product leader)
insights.so_what: The cost of building collapsing devalues upfront product-design deliberation in favor of rapid prototyping.
insights.quote: now it's actually faster to just build three versions and try them out

insights.claim: Expertise-based identity creates a personal innovator's dilemma: people keep doing what they are best at after the technology makes it less important, so product leaders must throw away what they know about themselves in the job every couple of months.
insights.speaker: Amy (Anthropic product leader)
insights.so_what: Adaptability, not accumulated craft, is the durable differentiator for talent.

insights.claim: Anthropic leaders recommend 'framing the chaos' rather than mapping exact roadmaps and careers in uncertainty, since over-planning locks you out of trying new things, while pairing that chaos with clear DRIs such as 'bet leads' in Labs who decide to double down or wind down.
insights.speaker: Amy (Anthropic product leader)
insights.so_what: Fast-moving orgs pair exploratory freedom with unambiguous decision owners.

insights.claim: Anthropic's stated design principle for agent-native software is that everything a human can do in the product an agent should also be able to do, which unlocks emergent behavior where agents piece together and proactively offer new workflows; very few products get this right today.
insights.speaker: Mike (Anthropic builder)
insights.so_what: Incumbent SaaS with UI-only functionality is structurally behind agent-native entrants.
insights.quote: everything a human could do an agent should be able to do as well

insights.claim: Anthropic's next stage beyond agent-native is malleable interfaces that the agent can reshape, and internally much of the software employees use is now built, maintained and iterated on by Claude, such as a Claude-generated project status UI for a team with four independent workstreams.
insights.speaker: Mike (Anthropic builder)
insights.so_what: Internal tooling is shifting from bought or built-by-acceleration-team software to Claude-generated bespoke software, a threat to horizontal internal-tool vendors.

insights.claim: Malleable Claude-built software raises unresolved questions about who may update data (humans clicking versus Claude in the background) and about data provenance.
insights.speaker: Mike (Anthropic builder)
insights.so_what: Data governance and provenance become product features when agents write to systems of record.

insights.claim: For SaaS companies deciding whether to add agents, the advice is to build shared primitives or plumbing so agents and the REST API use the same paths; products show when this was designed in versus bolted on, which is hard for apps built over 20 years.
insights.speaker: Mike (Anthropic builder)
insights.so_what: Legacy SaaS with entrenched architecture faces a costly retrofit to be agent-native.

themes.theme: Exploring the frontier while serving a broad base

insights.claim: Anthropic encourages overlapping parallel product bets and says the failure mode is over-constraining a product from a theory upfront; Amy would rather have five overlapping products than one overly constrained one, consolidating after product-market fit.
insights.speaker: Amy (Anthropic product leader)
insights.so_what: Expect messy, duplicative Anthropic product surfaces near term, followed by consolidation of winners.
insights.quote: I would much rather have like five overlapping products

insights.claim: Anthropic found that chat and Cowork had different memory systems, MCP setups and file storage, so a Foundations team built shared infrastructure such as portable memory, letting experimental surfaces feel complementary even when overlapping.
insights.speaker: Mike (Anthropic builder)
insights.so_what: Shared memory and context layers are becoming the moat across Anthropic's product surfaces.

insights.claim: Anthropic Labs treats a project that only proves models are not ready as a win if it is externalized as an eval, then retried with each new model; its 2024 computer use product was too slow and error-prone for automation or education, and running it in an eval harness showed Sonnet 3.7 as a leap in computer use.
insights.speaker: Mike (Anthropic builder)
insights.so_what: Parked projects plus evals let a lab detect capability step-changes early; computer-use agents became viable with a specific model release.

insights.claim: People get capability blind: they try a task once, conclude models cannot do it and never retest, yet new models improve in unexpected ways within about three months, and many users still judge AI using older models.
insights.speaker: Amy (Anthropic product leader)
insights.so_what: Skeptical assessments from users on stale models understate current capability; the adoption and capability gap is an opportunity.

insights.claim: In an audience poll, many attendees had used Fable while fewer had used Astra.
insights.speaker: Amy (Anthropic product leader)
insights.so_what: Rough anecdotal signal that the audience of product practitioners adopted Fable far more widely than Astra.

insights.claim: Instagram showed a strong power law in tab usage, with the main feed about 80% of use and Explore perhaps rising from 10% to 15%, so folding successful experiments into a product means defending the main experience and saying no to extra tabs or sidebar items.
insights.speaker: Amy (Anthropic product leader)
insights.so_what: Most usage concentrates in one primary surface, so new AI features should be integrated rather than added as tabs.
insights.quote: main feed was like 80% of the use

insights.claim: The unsolved problem of turning parallel AI experiments into a coherent product, whether as tabs or separate apps, is something neither Anthropic nor OpenAI has fully figured out.
insights.speaker: Amy (Anthropic product leader)
insights.so_what: Product packaging of AI capabilities remains an open competitive question across labs.

insights.claim: A team without conviction assigned to a manufactured product direction produces a poor product; Anthropic backs teams with high conviction in their own direction rather than assigning B-team explorations.
insights.speaker: Amy (Anthropic product leader)
insights.so_what: Bottom-up conviction determines which bets get resourced.
insights.quote: I've never been like successful tasking a team to go like take a product area that they're not excited about

insights.claim: Anthropic's stated goal for the coming year is closing the gap between what models can do and what most people use them for, so that researchers and business managers, not only heavy-agent software engineers, run long-horizon multi-agent work without feeling disempowered.
insights.speaker: Mike (Anthropic builder)
insights.so_what: Product-layer packaging, rather than raw model capability, is the main bottleneck to mass adoption.
insights.quote: the gap between what the models are capable of and like what most folks are using them for

insights.claim: Amy expects a year from now more small teams and solo builders starting businesses and building as AI tools make building easier, with benefits flowing to people who never use the tools directly.
insights.speaker: Amy (Anthropic product leader)
insights.so_what: Expect growth in solo-founder and small-team companies.
